claim: Adenosine to inosine (A-to-I) editing is a common post-transcriptional modification in RNA that occurs in a variety of organisms, including humans.
source: Adenosine to inosine (A-to-I) editing is a common post-transcriptional modification in RNA that occurs in a variety of organisms, including humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research and represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A-to-I deamination of specific adenosines in double-stranded RNA is catalyzed by enzymes called adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs).
source: This A-to-I deamination of specific adenosines in double-stranded RNA is catalyzed by enzymes called adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) (Melcher et al., 1996; Bass and Weintraub, 1988; Peng et al., 2012; Nishikura, 2016; Eggington et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 1989; Bass and Weintraub, 1987; Mannion et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2017; Tomaselli et al., 2015; Levanon et al., 2004; Schoft et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior research establishing the enzymatic mechanism.

claim: Inosine is structurally similar to guanosine and is interpreted as guanosine during translation and splicing.
source: Since inosine is structurally similar to guanosine, it is interpreted as a guanosine during the cellular processes of translation and splicing, thereby making ADARs powerful systems for altering protein sequences.
evidence: This claim is based on established biochemical knowledge about inosine structure and cellular interpretation.

claim: Adenosine deaminases have been repurposed for site-specific RNA editing by recruiting them to target RNA sequences using engineered ADAR-recruiting RNAs (adRNAs).
source: Correspondingly, adenosine deaminases have been repurposed for site-specific RNA editing by recruiting them to target RNA sequences using engineered ADAR-recruiting RNAs (adRNAs) (Woolf et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work demonstrating this approach.

claim: RNA-guided adenosine deaminases have demonstrated potential for correction of point mutations and repair of premature stop codons both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recently, several studies have demonstrated the potential of both genetically encodable and chemically modified RNA-guided adenosine deaminases for the correction of point mutations and the repair of premature stop codons both in vitro (Montiel-Gonzalez et al., 2013; Stafforst and Schneider, 2012; Cox et al., 2017; Wettengel et al., 2017; Merkle et al., 2019; Sinnamon et al., 2017; Monteleone et al., 2019; Fukuda et al., 2017; Qu et al., 2019) and in vivo (Katrekar et al., 2019; Sinnamon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating these capabilities.

claim: Exogenous ADARs introduce a significant number of transcriptome-wide off-target A-to-I edits.
source: These studies have primarily relied on exogenous ADARs which introduce a significant number of transcriptome-wide off-target A-to-I edits (Cox et al., 2017; Katrekar et al., 2019; Vallecillo-Viejo et al., 2018; Vogel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research documenting off-target effects.

claim: Using simple long antisense RNA (>60 bp) can recruit endogenous ADARs and these adRNAs are both genetically encodable and chemically synthesizable.
source: In this regard, we recently showed that using simple long antisense RNA (>60 bp) can suffice to recruit endogenous ADARs and these adRNAs are both genetically encodable and chemically synthesizable (Katrekar et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Engineered chemically synthesized antisense oligonucleotides can lead to robust RNA editing via endogenous ADAR recruitment.
source: and Merkle and colleagues showed that using engineered chemically synthesized antisense oligonucleotides (Merkle et al., 2019) could also lead to robust RNA editing via endogenous ADAR recruitment.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Endogenous ADAR recruitment is restricted to editing adenosines in certain RNA motifs preferred by native ADARs and in tissues with high endogenous ADAR activity.
source: Although this modality allows for highly specific editing, its applicability is restricted to editing adenosines in certain RNA motifs preferred by the native ADARs, and in tissues with high endogenous ADAR activity.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the properties of endogenous ADARs.

claim: Deamination of cytosine to uracil (C-to-U) editing requires exogenous delivery of ADAR2 variants.
source: Additionally, it cannot be utilized for novel functionalities such as deamination of cytosine to uracil (C-to-U) editing which requires exogenous delivery of ADAR2 variants (Abudayyeh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The crystal structure of the ADAR2 deaminase domain (ADAR2-DD) has been determined.
source: In this regard, the crystal structure of the ADAR2 deaminase domain (ADAR2-DD) (Macbeth et al., 2005; Matthews et al., 2016; Thuy-Boun et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The study performed a quantitative deep mutational scan (DMS) measuring the effect of every possible single amino acid substitution across 261 residues of the ADAR2-DD on enzyme function.
source: To address this, we first carried out a quantitative deep mutational scan (DMS), measuring the effect of every possible single amino acid substitution across 261 residues of the ADAR2-DD, on enzyme function.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The DMS enabled identification of novel enhanced variants for A-to-I editing.
source: We utilized the sequence-function map thus generated, to identify novel enhanced variants for A-to-I editing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results from the DMS.

claim: A genetically encodable split-ADAR2 system was engineered that enabled efficient and highly specific RNA editing.
source: Additionally, combining information from these sequence-function maps with existing knowledge of the structure and residue conservation scores, we also engineered a genetically encodable split-ADAR2 system that enabled efficient and highly specific RNA editing.
evidence: This claim describes the engineering approach and outcome demonstrated in the study.

claim: The DMS library comprised 4959 single amino acid variants (261 × 19) of the ADAR2-DD core residues 340-600.
source: By ensuring every cell in the pooled screen received a single library element, we could perform a quantitative DMS of the core 261 amino acids (residues 340–600) of the ADAR2-DD via 4959 (261 × 19) single amino acid variants, directly measuring the effect of each mutation on A-to-I editing yields
evidence: This claim describes the library design used in the study.

claim: 4958 of the 4959 possible variants were successfully detected in the DMS.
source: 4958 of the 4959 possible variants were successfully detected, of which 4931 elements had over 50 reads in each biological replicate and were included in the subsequent analysis
evidence: This claim reports the experimental coverage achieved in the DMS.

claim: The DMS replicates showed a correlation of R² = 0.687.
source: The deaminase domain transcripts for each variant also contained the associated A-to-I editing yields, which were then quantified for both replicates of the DMS (R2 = 0.687)
evidence: This claim is supported by the replicate correlation data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Most mutations in conserved regions 442-460 and 469-495 that bind the RNA duplex near the editing site led to a significant decrease in editing efficiency.
source: As expected, most mutations in conserved regions 442–460 and 469–495 that bind the RNA duplex near the editing site led to a significant decrease in editing efficiency of the enzyme (Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS data and cited structural information.

claim: Mutating the E488 residue to a positively charged or most polar-neutral amino acids resulted in an improvement in editing efficiency.
source: However, mutating the negatively charged E488 residue, which recognizes the cytosine opposite the flipped adenosine by donating hydrogen bonds, to a positively charged or most polar-neutral amino acids resulted in an improvement in editing efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS data.

claim: The E488Q mutation has been shown to improve the catalytic activity of the ADAR2 enzyme.
source: This is consistent with the previously discovered E488Q mutation which has been shown to improve the catalytic activity of the enzyme (Kuttan and Bass, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Most mutations to residues that contact the flipped adenosine (V351, T375, K376, E396, C451, R455) were detrimental to enzyme function.
source: Furthermore, most mutations to residues that contact the flipped adenosine (V351, T375, K376, E396, C451, R455) were observed to be detrimental to enzyme function (Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS data and cited structural information.

claim: Residues of the ADAR2-DD that interact with the zinc ion and inositol hexakisphosphate (R400, R401, K519, R522, S531, W523, D392, K483, C451, C516, H394, and E396) were extremely intolerant to mutations.
source: Similarly, the residues of the ADAR2-DD that interact with the zinc ion in the active site and the inositol hexakisphosphate (R400, R401, K519, R522, S531, W523, D392, K483, C451, C516, H394, and E396) were all also extremely intolerant to mutations (Macbeth et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS data and cited structural information.

claim: Surface exposed residues in general readily tolerated mutations as compared to buried residues.
source: Additionally, as expected, surface exposed residues in general readily tolerated mutations as compared to buried residues (Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the DMS data and cited structural information.

claim: The Pearson correlation between the arrayed validations and the DMS data was 0.818.
source: The Pearson correlation between the arrayed validations and the data obtained in the screen was 0.818 while the Spearman (rank) correlation was 0.824
evidence: This claim is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The Spearman (rank) correlation between the arrayed validations and the DMS data was 0.824.
source: The Pearson correlation between the arrayed validations and the data obtained in the screen was 0.818 while the Spearman (rank) correlation was 0.824
evidence: This claim is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: A screen was carried out to identify domain variants that improved editing at adenosines flanked by a 5' guanosine.
source: Building on this platform (Figure 1a, b, and c), we next screened for domain variants that improved editing at refractory RNA motifs such as adenosines flanked by a 5' guanosine (Vogel et al., 2018; Kuttan and Bass, 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The 5'-GAN-3' enhancer screen evaluated 3287 mutants for their ability to edit a GAC motif.
source: A screen was carried out in cell lines harboring these MS2-adRNAs by transducing them with the corresponding MCP-ADAR2-DD(E488Q) libraries at a low MOI (0.2–0.4), evaluating the potential of 3287 mutants to edit a GAC motif.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and scale.

claim: The 5'-GAN-3' enhancer screen replicates showed a correlation of R² = 0.476.
source: Similar to above, following lentiviral transduction and selection, RNA was extracted, reverse transcribed, and relevant regions of the deaminase domain amplified, sequenced, and analyzed (R2 = 0.476)
evidence: This claim is supported by the replicate correlation data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: A novel mutant E488Q, N496F was discovered that enhanced editing at a 5'-GAC-3' motif.
source: Via this approach, we discovered a novel mutant E488Q, N496F that enhanced editing at a 5'-GAC-3' motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data.

claim: In the ADAR2-DD(E488Q) crystal structure, the N496 residue is in close proximity to the adenosine on the unedited strand that base pairs with the 5' uracil flanking the target adenosine.
source: Interestingly, in the ADAR2-DD(E488Q) crystal structure, the N496 residue is in close proximity to the adenosine on the unedited strand that base pairs with the 5' uracil flanking the target adenosine (Figure 1g; Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural information shown in Figure 1g and cited literature.

claim: The E488Q, N496F double mutant was 3-fold better at restoring luciferase activity compared to E488Q alone.
source: We validated this mutant using a cypridina luciferase (cluc) reporter bearing a premature opal stop codon (UGA) and confirmed that the E488Q, N496F double mutant was 3-fold better at restoring luciferase activity as compared to E488Q alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The double mutant E488Q, N496F was 1.1- to 2.1-fold more efficient at editing various 5'-GAN-3' motifs compared to E488Q.
source: We observed that the double mutant E488Q, N496F was 1.1- to 2.1-fold more efficient at editing various 5'-GAN-3' motifs as compared to the E488Q (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 3b and c)
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 1h and supplementary figures.

claim: The E488Q, N496F variant was at least as efficient as E488Q at editing all other motifs, with improved editing also observed at 5'-NAC-3' motifs.
source: We also confirmed that this new variant was at least as efficient as the E488Q at editing all other motifs, with improved editing also observed at 5'-NAC-3' motifs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Overexpression of ADARs leads to promiscuous transcriptome-wide off-targeting due to their intrinsic dsRNA binding activity.
source: Due to their intrinsic dsRNA binding activity, overexpression of ADARs leads to promiscuous transcriptome-wide off-targeting
evidence: This claim is based on the known properties of ADARs and prior observations.

claim: Splitting the deaminase domain into two catalytically inactive fragments that come together to form a catalytically active enzyme only at the intended target could improve specificity.
source: We hypothesized that it might be possible to achieve this by splitting the deaminase domain into two catalytically inactive fragments that come together to form a catalytically active enzyme only at the intended target (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim represents the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: 18 putative regions for splitting the ADAR2-DD were identified based on DMS results, crystal structure, and residue conservation scores.
source: Examining the results of the DMS (focusing on sites with high mutability), as well as the crystal structure of the ADAR2-DD (focusing on high solvent accessible surface area), and residue conservation scores across species (focusing on low scores of conservation), we identified 18 putative regions for splitting the protein (Figure 2b; Matthews et al., 2016; Dagliyan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim describes the rational design approach combining multiple data sources.

claim: Split-ADAR2 pairs 9-12 showed the best editing efficiency and were all located within residues 465-468.
source: Of these pairs 9–12 showed the best editing efficiency, and notably were all located within residues 465–468 which have low conservation scores across species (Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Residues 465-468 have low conservation scores across species.
source: Of these pairs 9–12 showed the best editing efficiency, and notably were all located within residues 465–468 which have low conservation scores across species (Matthews et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited conservation analysis.

claim: The region containing residues 465-468 is flanked by highly conserved amino acids (442-460 and 469-495).
source: Interestingly, this region is flanked by highly conserved amino acids (442–460 and 469–495).
evidence: This claim is based on conservation analysis.

claim: Every component of the split-ADAR2 system was essential for RNA editing.
source: We also confirmed that every component of the split-ADAR2 system was essential for RNA editing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the component testing experiments.

claim: Editing of the RAB7A transcript and restoration of luciferase activity was observed only when every component of the split-ADAR2 system was delivered.
source: We observed editing of the RAB7A transcript and restoration of luciferase activity only when every component of the split-ADAR2 system was delivered, confirming that the individual components lacked enzymatic activity (Figure 3a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Fragment orientation is important for the formation of a functional split-ADAR2 enzyme.
source: Additionally, we also confirmed the importance of fragment orientation for the formation of a functional enzyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by the orientation testing experiments.

claim: Functionality was observed only for the MCP-ADAR2-DDN paired with ADAR2-DDC-λN.
source: We then tested each pair of N- and C-terminal fragments and observed functionality only for the MCP-ADAR2-DDN paired with ADAR2-DDC-λN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the orientation testing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A humanized split-ADAR2 system was created by replacing MCP and λN with the human TAR binding protein and stem loop binding protein, respectively.
source: Since MCP and λN are proteins of viral origin we next replaced these with the human TAR binding protein and the stem loop binding protein, respectively, to create a humanized split-ADAR2 system with improved translational relevance (Rauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the engineering approach for creating a humanized system.

claim: The humanized split-ADAR2 system showed restoration of luciferase activity in the presence of a chimeric adRNA containing a histone stem loop and a TAR stem loop.
source: In the presence of a chimeric adRNA containing a histone stem loop and a TAR stem loop, we observed restoration of luciferase activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The ADAR2-DD(E488Q) showed significantly high off-target editing compared to the ADAR2-DD.
source: As expected with hyperactive enzyme variants, the ADAR2-DD(E488Q) showed significantly high off-target editing as compared to the ADAR2-DD (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Splitting the deaminase domain resulted in a 1000- to 1300-fold reduction in the number of off-targets compared to the full-length ADAR2-DD or ADAR2-DD(E488Q).
source: Notably, by splitting the deaminase domain, we observed a 1000- to 1300-fold reduction in the number of off-targets as compared to the full-length ADAR2-DD or ADAR2-DD(E488Q) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The specificity profiles of the split-ADAR2 system were comparable to those seen when using endogenous recruitment of ADARs via long antisense RNA.
source: Excitingly, the specificity profiles of the split-ADAR2 system were comparable to those seen when using endogenous recruitment of ADARs via long antisense RNA (Katrekar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior data from the authors.

claim: The split-ADAR2 system showed robust editing efficiency at endogenous loci in CKB and KRAS.
source: To confirm generalizability of the results, we also tested the split-ADAR2 at two additional endogenous loci: an adenosine in the 3'UTR of CKB and an adenosine in the CDS of KRAS, and observed robust editing efficiency of the split-ADAR2 system (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: An all-in-one vector bearing a bicistronic ADAR2-DDC-λN-P2A-MCP-ADAR2-DDN enabled higher editing efficiencies across all three loci tested.
source: To enable convenient delivery of the split-ADAR2 system, we also created an all-in-one vector bearing a bicistronic ADAR2-DDC-λN-P2A-MCP-ADAR2-DDN which also enabled higher editing efficiencies across all three loci tested (Figure 3a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 3a and 3c.

claim: In the split-ADAR2 system, highly edited off-targets were guide RNA sequence dependent, in contrast to full-length deaminase domain overexpression where off-targets were predominantly deaminase domain driven.
source: A closer look at the off-targets revealed that in case of the split-ADAR2 system, highly edited off-targets were indeed guide RNA sequence dependent. This is in contrast to full-length deaminase domain overexpression where off-targets were predominantly deaminase domain driven (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of off-target patterns in the RNA-seq data.

claim: The entire split-ADAR2 system consisting of CMV promoter-driven ADAR2-DDC-λN-P2A-MCP-ADAR2-DDN and a human U6 promoter-driven BoxB-MS2 adRNA is ~3500 bp in size.
source: The entire split-ADAR2 system consisting of CMV promoter-driven ADAR2-DDC-λN-P2A-MCP-ADAR2-DDN and a human U6 promoter-driven BoxB-MS2 adRNA is ~3500 bp in size and can easily be packaged into a single adeno-associated virus (AAV).
evidence: This claim is based on calculation of the construct size.

claim: The split-ADAR2 system can easily be packaged into a single adeno-associated virus (AAV).
source: The entire split-ADAR2 system consisting of CMV promoter-driven ADAR2-DDC-λN-P2A-MCP-ADAR2-DDN and a human U6 promoter-driven BoxB-MS2 adRNA is ~3500 bp in size and can easily be packaged into a single adeno-associated virus (AAV).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the construct size and known AAV packaging capacity.

claim: A split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was created.
source: Lastly, to test if the split-ADAR2 chassis could be expanded to highly active ADAR variants that enable efficient editing of 5'-GAN-3' motifs as well as those that enable C-to-U editing, we created a split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) and a split-RESCUE (RNA Editing for Specific C-to-U Exchange) system (Abudayyeh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the engineering of a new variant.

claim: A split-RESCUE system was created.
source: Lastly, to test if the split-ADAR2 chassis could be expanded to highly active ADAR variants that enable efficient editing of 5'-GAN-3' motifs as well as those that enable C-to-U editing, we created a split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) and a split-RESCUE (RNA Editing for Specific C-to-U Exchange) system (Abudayyeh et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the engineering of a new variant.

claim: The split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was better at editing a GAC motif compared to the split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q).
source: We confirmed that the split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was indeed better at editing a GAC motif as compared to the split-ADAR2-DD(E488Q) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The full-length ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was highly promiscuous.
source: Although the full-length ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was highly promiscuous, splitting it enabled high transcriptome-wide specificity while targeting a UAG in the RAB7A transcript (Figure 4b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Splitting the ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) enabled high transcriptome-wide specificity while targeting a UAG in the RAB7A transcript.
source: Although the full-length ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) was highly promiscuous, splitting it enabled high transcriptome-wide specificity while targeting a UAG in the RAB7A transcript (Figure 4b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The split-RESCUE system showed comparable C-to-U RNA editing levels of the endogenous RAB7A transcript to the full-length MCP-RESCUE.
source: Additionally, we noted comparable C-to-U RNA editing levels of the endogenous RAB7A transcript using the split-RESCUE and the full-length MCP-RESCUE (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The split-RESCUE system was highly specific in both the A-to-I(G) and C-to-U space compared to the MCP-RESCUE.
source: However, the split-RESCUE system was also highly specific, both in the A-to-I(G) and C-to-U space as compared to the MCP-RESCUE (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The efficiency of the split-ADAR2 system was ~50-70% compared to full-length domain overexpression.
source: Due to this requirement of the split-domains to assemble, the efficiency of this system was ~50–70% compared to full-length domain overexpression
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of editing efficiencies between split and full-length systems.

claim: The split-ADAR2 tool was highly transcript specific (~1000-fold compared to full-length domain overexpression).
source: but the split-ADAR2 tool was highly transcript specific (~1000-fold compared to full-length domain over expression)
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq specificity data.

claim: The off-target profiles of split-ADAR2 were similar to those seen via recruitment of endogenous ADARs.
source: and notably with off-target profiles similar to those seen via recruitment of endogenous ADARs (Katrekar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior data.

claim: Replicate correlation values were negatively impacted because the screen was carried out in a lentiviral format.
source: While this novel screening approach was useful for creating an average mutagenesis map of the ADAR2-DD and identifying highly active variants, we believe that replicate correlation values were negatively impacted given that the screen was carried out in a lentiviral format.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' interpretation of the replicate correlation data.

claim: Lentivirus integrates randomly into the cell's genome, resulting in variability in ADAR2-DD transcript levels between different cells.
source: As lentivirus integrates randomly into the cell's genome, this results in variability in ADAR2-DD transcript levels between different cells.
evidence: This claim is based on known properties of lentiviral integration.

claim: The ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) showed increased bystander editing compared to the ADAR2-DD.
source: However, like the ADAR2-DD(E488Q), the ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) showed increased bystander editing and transcriptome-wide off-targeting as compared to the ADAR2-DD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the editing data.

claim: The ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) showed increased transcriptome-wide off-targeting compared to the ADAR2-DD.
source: However, like the ADAR2-DD(E488Q), the ADAR2-DD(E488Q, N496F) showed increased bystander editing and transcriptome-wide off-targeting as compared to the ADAR2-DD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data.

claim: The DMS library was created using six tiling oligonucleotide pools.
source: Given the large size of the deaminase domain at >750 bp, the library of ADAR variants was created using six tiling oligonucleotide pools (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim describes the library construction method.

claim: Members of the first three library pools were assayed for editing at the 5' end of the ADAR2-DD while the remaining members were assayed at the 3' end.
source: To ensure read length coverage in next generation sequencing, members of the first three library pools were assayed for editing at the 5' end of the ADAR2-DD while the remaining members were assayed at the 3' end (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design for sequencing coverage.

claim: Two HEK293FT clonal cell lines were created following high MOI transduction with lentivirus bearing two copies of MS2-adRNAs targeting either the 5' or the 3' UAG sites.
source: To minimize assay noise resulting from varying expression of the guide RNA in each cell, two HEK293FT clonal cell lines were created following a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) transduction with lentivirus bearing two copies of MS2-adRNAs targeting either the 5' or the 3' UAG sites integrated into them (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim describes the cell line creation method.

claim: The DMS was carried out by transducing cell lines harboring MS2-adRNAs with the corresponding ADAR mutant libraries at a low MOI of 0.2-0.4.
source: The DMS was carried out in cell lines harboring these MS2-adRNAs by transducing them with the corresponding ADAR mutant libraries at a low MOI of 0.2–0.4.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Two biological replicates were performed in independent plates of cells transduced with the lentiviral libraries.
source: Two biological replicates were performed in independent plates of cells transduced with the lentiviral libraries.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: 4931 elements had over 50 reads in each biological replicate and were included in the subsequent analysis.
source: 4958 of the 4959 possible variants were successfully detected, of which 4931 elements had over 50 reads in each biological replicate and were included in the subsequent analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim describes the data filtering criteria.

claim: 72% of the validated samples were not significantly different from the data obtained in the screen (p > 0.05).
source: p-Values were computed using Welch's t-test; 72% of the validated samples were not significantly different from the data obtained in the screen (p > 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by the validation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The study used HEK293FT cells that were authenticated by STR and tested for mycoplasma contamination by the vendor.
source: These cells were authenticated by STR and tested for mycoplasma contamination by the vendor.
evidence: This claim describes the cell line quality control.

claim: At least 1000× coverage was maintained at all steps of the screen.
source: At least 1000× coverage was maintained at all steps of the screen.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design parameter.

claim: RNA-seq samples were collected with 25 million uniquely aligned sequencing read pairs per sample.
source: From each sample, we collected 25 million uniquely aligned sequencing read pairs.
evidence: This claim describes the sequencing depth.

claim: Fisher's exact test was used to quantify significant changes in A-to-G editing yields relative to untransfected cells.
source: We then used Fisher's exact test to quantify significant changes in A-to-G editing yields, relative to untransfected cells, at each reference adenosine site having sufficient read coverage.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis method.
